'''''Taxus brevifolia''''', the '''Pacific yew''' or '''western yew''', is a [[species]] of [[conifer]] in the yew [[family (botany)|family]], [[Taxaceae]], native to the [[Pacific Northwest]] of [[North America]]. It is a small tree, thriving in moisture and otherwise tending to take the form of a [[shrub]].

==Description==
A small [[conifer]] (sometimes appearing as a [[shrub]]),<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle |pages=181–186 |language=en |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}}</ref> the Pacific yew grows {{convert|10–15|m|abbr=off}} tall and with a trunk up to {{convert|50|cm|abbr=off}} in diameter, rarely more. In some instances, trees with heights in excess of {{Cvt|20|m}} occur in parks and other protected areas, quite often in gullies. The tree is extremely slow-growing, and has a habit of rotting from the inside, creating hollow forms. This makes it difficult and sometimes impossible to make accurate [[Dendrochronology|ring counts]] to determine a specimen's true age. Often damaged by [[Ecological succession|succession]] of the forest, it usually ends up in a squat, multiple-leader form, able to grow new sprouts from decapitated stumps.<ref name=":02" /> In its shrub form, sometimes called "yew brush", it can reproduce vegetatively via [[layering (horticulture)|layering]].<ref name=":02" />

It has thin, scaly [[Bark (botany)|bark]], red then purplish-brown,<ref name=":02" /> covering a thin layer of off-white sap wood with a darker [[heartwood]] that varies in color from brown to a purplish hue to deep red, or even bright orange when freshly cut.<ref name=":02" /> The [[leaves]] are lanceolate, flat, dark green, {{Cvt|1–3|cm|frac=16}} long<ref name=":02" /> and {{convert|2–3|mm|frac=32}} broad, arranged spirally on the stem, but with the leaf bases twisted to align the leaves in two flat rows either side of the stem except on erect leading shoots where the spiral arrangement is more obvious.

The [[conifer cone|seed cones]] are highly modified, each cone containing a single [[seed]] {{Cvt|4–7|mm|frac=16}} long partly surrounded by a modified scale which develops into a soft, bright red [[Berry (botany)|berry]]-like structure called an [[aril]],<ref name=":02" /> {{Cvt|8–15|mm|frac=16}} long and wide and open at the end. The arils are mature 6–9 months after pollination. The seeds contained in the arils are eaten by [[Thrush (bird)|thrushes]], and other [[bird]]s, which disperse the hard seeds undamaged in their droppings; maturation of the arils is spread over 2–3 months, increasing the chances of successful seed dispersal. The male cones are globose, {{Cvt|3–6|mm|frac=16}} diameter, and shed their [[pollen]] in early spring. It is mostly [[dioecious]], but occasional individuals can be variably [[monoecious]], or change sex with time.{{Citation needed|reason=Citation needed for variability in sex|date=May 2018}}

== Taxonomy ==

=== Varieties ===

==== ''Taxus brevifolia'' var. ''reptaneta'' ====
''T. brevifolia'' var. ''reptaneta'' (thicket yew) is a shrub variety that generally occurs in the mid to upper elevation range of the typical variety, {{Convert|1000–1220|m|abbr=on}} at its southernmost occurrence in the [[Klamath Mountains]] region, and at lower elevations further north.<ref name="Spjut2007b">Spjut, R. W. 2007. Taxonomy and nomenclature of ''Taxus''.  J. Bot. Res. Inst. Texas 1(1): 203–289.</ref> It is distinguished from young trees of the typical variety (var. ''brevifolia'') by its stems initially creeping along the ground for a short distance before ascending (curving) upwards and by the branches growing off to one side of the stem, usually the upper side.<ref>Web page, World Botanical Associates, ''Taxus brevifolia'' var. ''reptaneta''; http://www.worldbotanical.com/taxus_brevifolia_var_reptaneta.htm. Retrieved 9 Dec 2014</ref> The epithet ''reptaneta'' is from the Latin ''reptans'' which means 'creeping, prostrate, and rooting',<ref>Stearn, W. T.  1983.  Botanical Latin.  3rd ed.  David & Charles, London</ref> which is exactly what this variety does; in rooting, it forms yew thickets; hence, the epithet ''reptaneta'' (-''etum'' means 'collective place of growth') and hence the common name, thicket yew.

Unlike the typical variety, thicket yew grows in abundance on open sunny avalanche shoots or ravines as well as in the forest understory. It also occurs along forest margins. In northwestern Montana, a variant of the thicket yew does not ascend upwards; rather, it remains along the ground.<ref name="Spjut2007b" /> This is probably the ancestral form; the upright form with branches along the upper side would be the expected growth pattern that might evolve from one with stems that strictly creep along the ground, since branches can only arise from the upper surface.

''T. brevifolia'' var. ''reptaneta'' has been described as synonymous with typical yew (var. ''brevifolia''). Though the two varieties may be genetically distinct, some botanists only use this taxon to describe different geographical ranges. For example, ''[[Taxus mairei|T. mairei]]'' var. ''speciosa'', which occurs with the typical variety in southern China in 10 of 13 provinces, was rejected for the lack of a "geographic reason" for recognition<ref>Möller M, Gao L-M, Mill RR, Liu J, Zhang D-Q, Poudel RC, Li D-Z, 2013. A multidisciplinary approach reveals hidden taxonomic diversity in the morphologically challenging ''Taxus wallichiana'' complex. Taxon 62: 1161–1177.</ref> though it appears genetically distinct.<ref>Gao L-M, Möller M, Zhang X-M, Hollingsworth ML, Liu J, Mill RR, Gibby M, Li D-Z, 2007. High variation and strong phylogeographic pattern among cpDNA haplotypes in ''Taxus wallichiana'' (Taxaceae) in China and North Vietnam. Molec. Ecol. 16: 4684–4698.</ref> ''T. brevifolia'' var. ''reptaneta'' has also been proposed to be elevated to a [[subspecies]], despite that rank being used to define geographically separated groups of ''T. baccata''.<ref>Pilger R, 1903. Taxaceae-Taxoideae—Taxeae. ''Taxus''. In: Das Pflanzenreich IV (Engler A. ed.): 110–116.</ref>{{efn|Further, one recommendation strongly discourages taxonomists from "elevating a 'variety' to a 'subspecies' unless there is sufficient scientific evidence to warrant such an elevation," and that "it is crucial to provide continuity."<ref>Ellison AM, Davis CC, Calie PJ, Naczi RFC, 2014. Pitcher plants (''Sarracenia'') provide a 21st-century perspective on infraspecific ranks and interspecific hybrids: A modest proposal for appropriate recognition and usage. Syst. Bot. 39: 939–949.</ref>}}

==== ''Taxus brevifolia'' var. ''polychaeta'' ====
Typical ''T. brevifolia'', like most species in the genus, usually produces a single ovule on a complex scaly shoot, composed of a primary shoot and a secondary short shoot. To the casual observer, they appear as one funnelform shoot with an ovule at the apex.<ref>Florin R, 1951. Evolution in cordaites and conifers. Acta Horti Berg. 16: 285–388, plate</ref> ''T. brevifolia'' var. ''polychaeta'' differs from var. ''brevifolia'' in producing a relatively longer primary shoot<ref name="Spjut2007b" /> with as many five secondary shoots.<ref>Web page, World Botanical Associates, Overview of the genus ''Taxus'', http://www.worldbotanical.com/TAXNA.HTM, retrieved 9 Dec 2014</ref> The epithet, ''polychaeta'', is in reference to the primary shoot resembling a [[polychaete]] worm; hence, its common name 'worm cone yew'. Variety ''polychaeta'' appears to be relatively rare. It may have been [[Local extinction|extirpated]] from the type locality—around [[Mud Bay, Thurston County, Washington|Mud Bay]] near [[Olympia, Washington]]—as a result of urban expansion. It is also known from Northern Idaho and [[Sonoma County, California]].<ref name="Spjut2007b" /><ref>Web page, World Botanical Associates, ''Taxus brevifolia'' var. ''polychaeta''; http://www.worldbotanical.com/taxus_brevifolia_var_polychaeta.htm; retrieved 9 Dec 2014</ref>

As in the case with thicket yew, worm yew has been reported to be the same as the typical variety; however, there are no specific studies to support this conclusion. The authority of the thicket yew and worm cone yew has been involved in the study of ''Taxus'' for 25 years at the time the varieties were described.<ref name="Spjut2007b" /><ref>Spjut, R. W.  1977. === Similar species ===
Yew foliage is very similar to that of ''[[Sequoia sempervirens]]'', the coastal redwood.<ref name=":02" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
Pacific yew is [[native species|native]] to the [[Pacific Northwest]]. It ranges from southernmost [[Alaska]] south to [[Northern California]], mostly in the [[Pacific Coast Ranges]], but with isolated [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct]] populations in southeast [[British Columbia]] and in [[Northern Idaho]].<ref name="Bolsinger1965">

Brigham Young University Press, Provo.</ref> It grows in varying types of environments; however, in drier environments it is mostly limited to stream-side habitats, whereas in moist environments it will grow up onto slopes and ridgetops,<ref name="Bolsinger1965" /> at least as high in altitude as {{Convert|1400|m}} above sea level.<ref name=":02" /> Pacific yew is [[shade tolerant]], but can also grow in sun.<ref name="Mitchell">{{cite journal |last=Mitchell |first=A. |year=1998 |title=Acclimation of Pacific yew (Taxus brevifolia) foliage to sun and shade |url=http://treephys.oxfordjournals.org/content/18/11/749.full.pdf+html |journal=Tree Physiology |volume=18 |issue=11 |pages=749–757 |doi=10.1093/treephys/18.11.749 |pmid=12651409 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The tree's shade tolerance allows it to form an [[understory]], which means that it can grow along streams providing shade to maintain water temperature.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Scher |first1=Stanley |last2=Schwarzschild |first2=Bert |year=1989 |title=Pacific Yew: a Faculative Riparian Conifer with an Uncertain Future |url=http://gis.fs.fed.us/psw/publications/documents/psw_gtr110/psw_gtr110_d_scher.pdf}}</ref>

==Ecology==

Birds eat the fruit cups and spread the seeds.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=Stephen |title=Western Forests (The Audubon Society Nature Guides) |date=1985 |publisher=Knopf |location=New York |isbn=0-394-73127-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/364 364] |url=https://archive.org/details/westernforests00whit/page/364 }}</ref> Moose feed on the tree in winter in forests of the [[Rocky Mountains]].<ref name=":02" />

==Toxicity==
Many parts of yews are poisonous and can be fatal if eaten, including the seed, which should not even be chewed.<ref name=":0" /> Ingestion of the Pacific yew can result in complex cardiac arrhythmia and hemodynamic instability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Temple |first=Courtney |last2=Lopez |first2=Annette |date=2023-12-31 |title=Fatal ingestion of Taxus brevifolia (Pacific yew): a case report |journal=Toxicology Communications |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=2220532 |doi=10.1080/24734306.2023.2220532|doi-access=free }}</ref>  

==Uses==

Traditionally, the resilient and rot-resistant wood was used by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] to make tools, bows (backed with sinew), arrows, and canoe paddles.<ref name=":02" /> Other purposes for yew included making harpoons, fishhooks, wedges, [[Club (weapon)|clubs]], spoons, drums, snowshoes, and arrowheads.<ref name=":02" /> The foliage and bark were used for medicinal purposes.<ref name=":02" /> Members of the [[Pit River Tribe]] would sell this plant to the [[Yuki people|Ukiah]].<ref>Chestnut, V. K. 1902 Plants Used by the Indians of Mendocino County, California. Contributions from the U.S. National Herbarium 7:295-408. (p. 305)</ref> The [[Maidu#Local divisions|Concow tribe]] calls the tree '''yōl'-kō''' ([[Konkow language]]).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Chesnut | first1 =Victor King | author1-link=Victor King Chesnut |title=Plants used by the Indians of Mendocino County, California|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vLkUAAAAYAAJ|access-date=24 August 2012|year=1902|publisher=[[United States Government Printing Office|Government Printing Office]]|page = 408}}</ref>

Modern-day [[longbow]] makers report that a tiny percentage of yew trees are of a grain suitable for their craft.<ref name=":02" /> The [[Japanese carpentry|Japanese]] have used the wood for decorative purposes,<ref name="Bolsinger1965" /> and the Taiwanese have valued it as well.<ref name=":02" />

The juicy red cup around the seed seems to be edible (but not the toxic seed within),<ref name=":0" /> with a mild cherry [[jello]]-like flavour.<ref name=":02" /> The berry is said to have a sweet taste but slimy texture, while the leaves, bark, and seed are extremely poisonous and should not be consumed.<ref>{{cite book |last=MacKinnon |first=Andy |title=Edible and Medicinal Plants of Canada |publisher=Lone Pine Publishing |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-55105-572-5 |page=78}}</ref>

The [[chemotherapy]] drug [[paclitaxel]] (taxol), used in [[breast cancer|breast]], [[ovarian cancer|ovarian]], and [[lung cancer]] treatment, can be derived from ''T. brevifolia''<ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |page=104}}</ref> and other species of yew. As it was already becoming scarce when its chemotherapeutic potential was realized around the 1990s, the Pacific yew was never commercially harvested from its habitat at a large scale; the widespread use of paclitaxel was enabled circa 2003 when a semi-synthetic pathway was developed from extracts of cultivated yews of other species.<ref name=":02" />
